III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00826

That is why, in answer to fashionable theological movements that condemn everything they call gnosis without clearly understanding what spiritual knowledge is (see pp. 25 onward), we must say that it matters now more than ever. For anyone who knows through spiritual insight, as for the Qur'an itself, the cry “God is dead” is meaningless. The absurd, by definition, is what has no meaning. It would be absurd to imagine that divine truth depends on some particular moment in History, or that the truth revealed in a sacred book depends on the date when it appeared among the outward facts and passing circumstances of the world. We have heard the Imams themselves say as much.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00827

Spiritual events—the entirely real events of sacred history—do not belong to the past in the way that outward, material events do. Because they do not take place within that kind of time, later outward history cannot make them obsolete. They belong to the time of the soul (see Chapter IV, Section 5, and Book IV, Chapter II). In that time they are both present and still to come.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00828

The word “irreversible,” so often repeated without much thought, loses its force. In Semitic languages, the completed form of a verb does not simply correspond to the past tense in our languages. Depending on the context, it may be translated as past, present, or future. Even the events of the final fulfilment of history are described in this completed form.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00829

There is a relentless urge today to force spiritual events into material History—to make them “take place” in the ordinary record of visible facts—because we have grown unable to recognise the reality of events that cannot be entered into a public chronicle. Sacred history offers a different way of understanding them. Its events belong to outward history only as a ray of sunlight passing through stained glass belongs to the building it illuminates. Their truth raises those who witness them towards worlds in which their presence endures, complete and still present.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00830

This is precisely what the experience of a sacred book presupposes. It is also why the question of secularisation may ultimately turn on how we understand the sacred book itself. Secularisation begins with a refusal of haqiqat, a refusal to recognise the full depth and range of the book's meanings. The Imams' way of uncovering those meanings restores that fullness. Seen in this light, the deepest insight of Shiism comes more clearly into view.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00831
Chapter IV The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
en-book-1-ch-4-s1
1. The Sacred Book and Its Interpretation
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00832

In the preceding pages, we have often spoken of what I have called the “phenomenon of the Sacred Book”: what makes it distinctive, what makes it a complete reality in its own right, and how it gives Shiism its particular character. For Shiism is defined by the way it interprets the Book. The holy Imams are the guardians and guides of that interpretation; they are at once the keepers of the treasure and the treasure itself. Its inner principles open up entire worlds of meaning—worlds in which Nietzsche’s cry that “God is dead” would announce only the spiritual death of the person who utters it.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00833

We are dealing with spiritual realities that have their counterparts in every religious community gathered around a Sacred Book—the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab). The questions they raise have parallels from one tradition to another.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00834

Yet the traditions have not all reached the same degree of clarity about those questions, or studied them with equal care. This matters enormously. I therefore want to sketch the connections among these shared lines of inquiry, however briefly. My hope is that an Iranian reader interested in Western discussions, and a Western reader who wants to connect the interpretation of the Qur’an with questions already familiar to them, can both take part in the same conversation. These few preliminary remarks will help us understand the inner dimensions of religion and spiritual interpretation, which we will discuss in Chapter V, as well as the Shiite understanding of prophecy, which follows in Chapter VI.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00835

The Qur’anic expression Ahl al-Kitab literally means “People of the Book.” Strictly speaking, it describes a religious community that possesses a Sacred Book—a community whose very existence arises from that Book. Its religion rests on a text believed to have “come down from Heaven,” revealed to a prophet who was sent to teach it to the people entrusted to him. Alongside Muslims, the People of the Book are, above all, Jews and Christians. Zoroastrians have, to some extent, been granted the same standing because of the Avesta. The group known as the “Sabians of Harran,” who followed Hermetic teachings, were less fortunate.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00836

All these communities face the same fundamental problem. They have a Sacred Book that guides their lives and their understanding, both in this world and beyond it. Their first and final task is to understand that Book.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00837

But what does it mean to understand something, or to help someone else understand it? This is what the word hermeneutics, from the Greek hermeneia, refers to: the work of interpretation. Whenever we understand something, we understand a meaning. Here the aim must be to discover the Book’s true meaning.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00838

But how we understand depends on who we are—on our very way of being. A revealed Sacred Book therefore raises more than a question about this or that human action. It raises a question about what it means to be human at all. In philosophical terms, it calls our whole understanding of the human person into question.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00839

A believer’s inner life grows out of the meaning they find in the Book. Their lived situation is therefore one of interpretation: the true meaning comes to light for them, and in that same moment gives truth to their own existence. This is why the phenomenon of the Sacred Book shapes not only a particular view of human nature but an entire form of culture.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00840

Its effects are lasting. Indeed, the Sacred Book and the inner life that both gives rise to its interpretation and is shaped by it could provide a starting point for a comparison of spiritual life, or more broadly of religious understandings of the human person, among the peoples of the Book in East and West. The Bible and the Qur’an share more than certain teachings about prophecy.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00841

The search for a true spiritual meaning has also raised comparable questions for Christian and Muslim interpreters. This becomes especially clear when we look at Qur’anic stories that have earlier counterparts in the Bible, including books usually called “apocryphal.” Those who meditate on these stories often find themselves facing similar problems of interpretation. We are led, then, towards the idea of a comparative study of spiritual interpretation: a theology of the religions of the Book that would explore what they have in common, both in what a revealed Scripture demands of its readers and in what it allows them to discover.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00842

Imagine gathering the spiritual interpreters of biblical revelation and those of Qur’anic revelation in one ideal assembly—for the moment, perhaps, in a “castle of the soul,” a House of Wisdom (Domus Sapientiae). What would it mean to bring them together, and what might they discover? Elsewhere I have made a first attempt at such a comparison, using the figures of Adam and Noah as they appear in Swedenborg’s spiritual reading of the Bible and in Ismaili interpretations of Islamic revelation. Some of the parallels are remarkable.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00843
Sacred Books tell of people and events whose outward form (zahir) belongs to the past. They present figures, actions, and stories from earlier times.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00844

Yet these people and events must mean something different from what they would mean in an ordinary history book. If they matter to the life and death of the person reading them, they cannot be nothing more than events recorded in an old chronicle. We have already seen how important this was to the Shiite Imams. The Fifth Imam, Muhammad Baqir (d. 115 AH/733 CE), strongly told his companions: “If the revelation of the Qur’an had meaning only for the person or group of people because of whom a particular verse was revealed, the entire Qur’an would be dead today.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00845

“But no! The Sacred Book, the Qur’an, is alive and never dies. Its verses will come true for people in the future, just as they came true for people in the past.” With these words, the holy Imam was already avoiding the trap of what we would now call historicism: treating a sacred text as though its meaning were exhausted by the historical circumstances in which it first appeared.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00846

Consider the Latin word comprehendere, which originally includes the senses “to contain” and “to involve.” To understand a meaning is, in one way or another, to involve ourselves in it, to make it part of our own way of being. Anyone who has not taken that meaning into themselves—who has not truly understood it—will find it hard to explain it to someone else.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00847

And what if the meaning at stake is the meaning of that person’s own life? The verses of the Qur’an are called signs (ayat), and this is exactly the point: we are asked to understand signs addressed to us. Such understanding must happen now, in the present. The sign’s meaning lives in the person who understands it, because that person is the one to whom it speaks.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00848

At the heart of understanding, then, lies a problem of time: the relationship between the time of the events described and the time of the reader who interprets them. That relationship is itself the time and place where the two meet. If we ignore or refuse to face the problem, we miss the encounter. If we recognise it and try to work through it, we begin to examine honestly the assumptions behind every act of interpretation. This becomes especially urgent when what we are interpreting is a text regarded as a revealed Sacred Book.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00849

Later (§ 5) we will see that Islamic spiritual thinkers distinguished different qualities of time. They recognised a special kind of time involved in understanding events that unfold “within the soul.” And to speak of events “within the soul” is also to imply that they take place in spaces proper to the soul—in a world with its own kind of location.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
en-book-1-ch-4-s2
2. The Spaces and Perspectives of Spiritual Interpretation
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00850

Perhaps the better we become at seeing events as points in the one-way flow of historical time—dating them, placing them in a sequence, and explaining them through their place in that sequence—the harder it becomes to see them in another way. We may lose the ability to locate them in a space that is not the measurable, uniform space of the physical world: a space where their meaning depends on their enduring place within an ordered pattern of higher and lower levels. As we will see in Chapter V, Shiite interpretation of the Qur’an unfolds the text’s meanings across what we might call several levels of reality, which can even be represented in diagrams.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00851

Jewish Kabbalists and Christian thinkers who seek the inner meaning of the Bible do something similar. There seems to be a basic difference between this way of seeing and what we ordinarily call historical understanding. The two could perhaps be related if we had a way to show how the patterns in one correspond to those in the other. A spiritual interpreter may possess such a method. It is far less clear that a historian, working strictly as a historian, does.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00852

Consider an example that brings the problem of spiritual interpretation into sharp focus, for the Bible and therefore for the Qur’an as well. In one of his major works, where he sets out his theology and philosophy of divine wisdom most systematically, Emanuel Swedenborg (1688–1772) describes the principle behind his reading of Scripture. Just as there are three Heavens in the spiritual world—the highest, middle, and lowest Heavens—there are three corresponding meanings within the divine Word: a heavenly meaning, a spiritual meaning, and a natural meaning.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00853

What comes first and is most fundamental lies at the centre and becomes the ultimate purpose, just as an end is already present in its cause and therefore in its effect. The Word has an outer natural, or literal, meaning. This is the covering, the vessel, and the support of an inner spiritual meaning. That spiritual meaning, in turn, contains a meaning deeper still: the heavenly meaning. In Islamic inner teaching, this would correspond to what is called “the inner meaning of the inner meaning” (batin al-batin).
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00854

Both inner meanings are present at the same time within the literal meaning. Swedenborg then explores what such coexistence involves. In Heaven and in the world, he says, things can be arranged in two different ways. One is a successive order, where parts follow one another from highest to lowest. The other is a simultaneous order, where the parts are arranged from the innermost to the outermost, as though in concentric circles spreading towards their edge. Imagine the successive order as a column in a temple, narrower at the top and gradually widening towards the base.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00855

What is highest and comes first in that vertical order corresponds to what is most central and inward in the simultaneous order. What comes last, at the base of the successive order, corresponds to the outer edge of the simultaneous order.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00856

To picture how one arrangement becomes the other, imagine the highest and earliest parts of the successive order becoming the inmost heart of the simultaneous order. Meanwhile, the lowest and latest parts become its outermost regions. It is as though the column were to slide down into itself, like the sections of a telescope, until it became a flat surface. The column’s top would now occupy the centre.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00857

According to Swedenborg, this correspondence between sequence and coexistence—and the way coexistence arises from sequence—can be found throughout the material and spiritual worlds. The principle is constant: what is highest and first moves towards the innermost centre, where the ultimate purpose is found. In the divine Word, heavenly, spiritual, and natural meanings unfold in succession, but finally coexist in a single structure. The heavenly and spiritual meanings are both present within the natural or literal meaning, which contains and shelters them.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00858

The great Swedish visionary could hardly have made the problem of Scripture’s many meanings clearer. It is, at heart, a problem of how forms arranged in time relate to forms arranged in space. Only by posing the question in this way can we begin to imagine an other history, distinct from the material history of outward, observable facts. It also helps us avoid confusing spiritual meaning with allegory.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00859

Swedenborg opens up to spiritual understanding the spaces in which “events in Heaven” take place and can be perceived. By showing how events that follow one another can also exist together, he may be revealing a secret of the deepest spiritual life. It is the same secret suggested in Richard Wagner’s final opera, when Gurnemanz answers Parsifal: “I have scarcely taken a step, yet already I feel so far away!” “You see, my son,” Gurnemanz replies, “here time becomes space.”
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00860

This correspondence between forms in time and forms in space is a remarkably subtle example of two different structures sharing the same underlying pattern—what we might call isomorphism. It also suggests that there are several kinds of space. The space we perceive with our physical eyes may not even be the most important. After all, what concerns us in interpretation is the divine Word. It is a sound, a calling that brings beings into presence and remains their deepest, hidden nature. Once this nature has taken form in a being, it cannot be seen with ordinary eyesight. It reveals itself to another kind of sight, an inner vision able to perceive other spaces.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00861

Yet these are still spaces, with their own properties, different from those of the physical world. We therefore need to understand how the space of sound corresponds to those worlds beyond the senses, where the vibrations of the Word spread like “arpeggios laden with distant lights,” to borrow Joseph Baruzi’s phrase.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00862

It seems, in the end, that this way of seeing the inner and spiritual meanings of Scripture as present together with its outer and natural meaning is common to the great mystical traditions of divine wisdom that have arisen in religions based on revealed Books. As I have already suggested, there is something shared between Swedenborg’s reading of the Bible and the ways Twelver and Ismaili Shiites, or Sufis from Ibn Arabi’s school, read the Qur’an and the traditions that explain it.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00863

We can identify this common ground only by looking at the structures of their experience. It may take a careful study of how consciousness forms and recognises meaningful patterns to see what is happening and why it matters. Here I can only point to a few signposts.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00864

One particularly promising place to look is the philosophy of light developed in both Christian Europe and the Islamic East, especially Iran, during the same broad period. The spiritual challenges faced in the two traditions already show a similar underlying pattern. Their ideas about light may help us discover its foundation.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00865

As Étienne Gilson observed, the heavenly hierarchies described in writings attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite and the study of optics developed by Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) seem closely connected: the ordered outpouring of divine illumination and the philosophy of light belong together. The same is certainly true of Suhrawardi’s (d. 587 AH/1191 CE) “Eastern philosophy of divine wisdom.” Its foundations are a philosophy of light and an ordered world of archangels, drawing on both later Neoplatonism and the ancient Persian Zoroastrian tradition of divine wisdom (see Book II below).
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00866

Medieval thinkers’ interest in optics, and especially in works on perspective derived from Arabic texts, grew from this joining of the science of light with the philosophy of divine illumination. Robert Grosseteste was a leading figure in bringing the two together. In his account of the origin of the universe, light is the very substance of being. It is the first and most subtle form of bodily existence, the original principle from which worlds take shape. His treatise On Light, or the Beginning of Forms (De luce seu de inchoatione formarum) has an exact parallel in the teachings of Suhrawardi’s school, the Ishraqiyun, thinkers devoted to the wisdom of light or “Eastern wisdom.”
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00867

The laws of optics themselves open up the space—or perhaps the higher-dimensional space—needed to understand how spiritual meanings can be hidden within things we perceive with our senses. In his On Light, Bartholomew of Bologna (twelfth century) places the seven ways physical bodies receive light alongside the seven ways angelic and human minds share in divine Light. We might compare these in turn with the seven inner levels of the Qur’an, which the Sufi thinker Simnani links to seven subtle centres or organs of spiritual perception, each marked by its own colour and degree of light (see Book IV, Chapter IV).
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00868

We can now understand Roger Bacon’s extraordinary praise of perspective. For him, it is the most fundamental of the natural sciences, the key to intellectual knowledge and the spiritual sciences alike. Why? Because both concern a kind of seeing. The laws and images of outward illumination help us understand what happens when light reaches us inwardly. This is also why thinkers paid such close attention to geometrical figures, particularly the sphere and the pyramid, and to their properties. They could turn these shapes into symbols by relating them to the nature of light.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00869

A kind of map of the spiritual worlds then becomes possible. In Shiite teachings on divine wisdom, for example, Qazi Sa'id Qummi argues that there must be exactly twelve Imams. He bases this on twelve functional relationships that determine the shape of the cosmic Temple or “Throne,” regarded as the original pattern of the Kaaba’s cubic form. The diagrams found throughout Ismaili works and the writings of Ibn Arabi’s school—like those in the Kabbalah or the work of certain followers of Jacob Boehme—may look fantastic at first.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00870

In fact, they possess both strict internal order and real value for understanding. They show and test patterns that, for their authors, are real and are perceived through a particular way of knowing. The safest way to appreciate these diagrams is to follow the approach shared by philosophies of light in Iran and the West: to read the laws of optics and perspective for their inner spiritual meaning, against the background of a shared account of the universe’s origin in light.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00871

Of course, I am not suggesting that spiritual worlds can be reduced to the familiar rules of visual perspective. Quite the opposite. What matters is a turning back, a return to the very source of every perspective. That is why Suhrawardi and those who followed him so often appeal to the science of mirrors or use the mirror as an image.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00872

If mirrors can help us discover principles of structure that point towards the kind of space opened by spiritual interpretation, we might also have much to learn from those who study the experience of music. This would bring us back onto the path opened by the philosophers of light themselves, when they found a spiritual meaning in the laws of perspective.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00873

One influence on my thinking here has been the work of our late friend Victor Zuckerkandl. I have in mind especially the pages where he describes a room of mirrors: a room with mirrors on every side. He suggests that it offers an excellent way of understanding how a particular feature of musical experience shares the same structure as the mirror effects so often invoked by our visionary thinkers.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00874

I am thinking especially of a tradition reported by Ibn Arabi in his account of the mystery of the “heavenly Earth.” This is the world of pure imaginative perception, where God has created a universe corresponding to every individual soul. When a mystic looks into that universe, the mystic sees their own soul reflected there.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00875

Ibn Arabi says that this was what Abd Allah ibn Abbas, one of the best-known companions of the Prophet and the First Imam, meant when he declared: “This Kaaba [the sanctuary in Mecca] is only one dwelling among fourteen. In each of the seven Earths there is a being who is our image. In each of the seven Earths, therefore, there is an Ibn Abbas who is my image.”
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00876

This is surely one way these writers expressed their experience of a whole series of worlds, arranged in an order and corresponding to one another. Their inner experience allowed them to be present, in some way, in those different worlds.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00877

Yet this outlook feels so strange to us today, so distant from our ordinary habits of thought and our sense of the universe, that we will have to renew our methods of inquiry if we are even to begin to understand such an experience.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00878

We must find a way to give it the recognition its participants mean by tahqiq: to establish its reality as an experience. Otherwise we are left with explanations that reduce it to history, psychology, or a particular theory of social and intellectual change, whether dialectical or not. If we refuse those reductions, there is no avoiding the urgency of the task.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00879

We may find it easier to make the passage—the exodus—from the space of the senses into spaces beyond the senses if we study the problem directly. The relationship between the space of hearing and the space of sight gives us a way to do so. Seen from another angle, this is the relationship between forms in time and forms in space—or, in Swedenborg’s language, between successive order and simultaneous order.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00880

What struck me in Zuckerkandl’s discussion was his account of the room of mirrors as the place where visual and audible space come closest together. What happens in that room? Two things. First, we find repetition: things multiply themselves.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00881
Second, we find a movement that, even as it advances, returns to its starting point. I will call this a return or reversal, as I did earlier on page 143.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00882

First, in a room of mirrors, every object appears again and again, reflected from one mirror into another. No object is present in only one lonely place. Its appearance in one position immediately implies its appearance in others, multiplied into as many images as the mirrors and their reflections make possible. Something similar happens in the space of music. A sound is repeated from octave to octave. Its presence at one pitch is accompanied by its recurrence at the corresponding pitch in each successive octave. In fact, an entire musical key, with all its relationships, repeats from octave to octave, just as the whole room reappears again and again in its mirrors.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00883
We can sing the same hymn in different keys. The notes will be higher or lower, and therefore different in pitch, yet the tune remains unmistakably the same.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00884

This brings us to Zuckerkandl’s suggestion that musical experience lies at the very origin of the theory of Gestalt: the study of a form or pattern as a whole, rather than as a collection of separate pieces. How can a melody remain the same when the notes that make up its physical sound have changed? We discover that the melody’s essential “material” is not the individual notes but the relationships between them. The tune is preserved because those relationships remain the same.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00885

This principle of preservation is the key, I think, to understanding the basic rule that governs both Swedenborg’s reading of the Bible and the inner Islamic interpretation of the Qur’an and its vast collection of traditions. The same story can truly happen again on different levels, as though it were being played at ever-higher octaves, until we reach the level of events beyond ordinary history. Swedenborg does this when he interprets Genesis, Exodus, and Revelation.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00886

Twelver and Ismaili Shiites do something comparable when they recognise the spiritual meanings of Qur’anic verses and traditions at the level of the eternal company of the holy Imams, and of the ranks of spiritual beings that proceed from them (see Chapter V below). Without this idea of worlds repeating the same essential relationships at different levels, we could not understand the spiritual body or “resurrection body” described in our own time by the Shaykhi school of Shiism.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00887

At each higher octave, the defining relationships of a person, a situation, or an event remain intact, even though they appear in a different form. If we approach interpretation in terms of Gestalt, we may also see why modern empirical scholarship so often meets the entire practice of spiritual interpretation with indifference, rejection, or even hostility. It sees only arbitrary readings where there is, for those who practise this interpretation, an organic necessity of form. Perhaps there is such a thing as being deaf to meaning, just as there is such a thing as being tone-deaf.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00888

Second, the very structure of musical space seems to impose a law of return. Any movement away from a note on the musical scale can lead us forward until we arrive again at that same note, an octave higher. In the room of mirrors, too, each movement outward from a point is also a movement towards that point as it appears in a reflected image.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00889

In our musical system, the interval of a fifth—the dominant—marks the furthest point from the opening, fundamental note. From there the direction changes. The movement forward becomes a return to the starting note at the octave. It is understandable that people have spoken of the “miracle of the octave,” something apparently without parallel elsewhere in the world of phenomena.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00890

Yet if we look at the relationships involved, we find a similar pattern in the cycle that governs the origin and final destiny of the universe in Islamic inner teaching. Its two key terms are mabda' and ma'ad: the point of origin and the place of return (see page 127 above). The movement between them is not a straight line of development but a return.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00891

Our world’s course takes the form of a cycle: it goes back to its source, to the very level where the “drama in Heaven” gave rise to this passing material universe. The children of Adam have ahead of them the heavenly state they left behind them. Just so, as we move upwards through an octave, the starting note we have left behind is also the note towards which we are climbing.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00892

To set out from any point in the visible earthly world—the molk—is therefore to move towards its origin. The first destination is the world of Hurqalya, the mundus imaginalis, or intermediate world. Here the spiritual takes on body and form, while bodily things become spiritual, appearing as independent Forms and Images.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00893

Our authors repeatedly tell us that these forms have no need of any material substance apart from their own light, just as a mirror image seems to exist through light alone. This is also the basis of the multiplied presences described in Ibn Arabi’s tradition quoted above. It corresponds to what the study of sacred images calls different “levels of meaning.” Take the story of the holy Shiite Imams, who began the cycle of spiritual initiation that follows the cycle of prophecy (see Chapter VI and Book VII below).
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00894
We can understand their story at the level of earthly life—which, for us modern readers, is usually simply the level of history.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00895

But we can also understand it across one intermediate world after another, all the way to the highest spiritual fullness (see Chapter V). It is no coincidence that Ismaili thought arranges the Imams in groups of seven, just as it arranges prophecy in a pattern of seven, rising through one octave after another.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00896
Someone may object that this reading of music rests, in the end, on the tonal system that developed in the West and on our understanding of how harmony works.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00897

But that is precisely the point. It is especially we in the West who need to begin with the means already available to us and find our way back to an experience that opens up a different kind of space from the one we inhabit every day. That experience might allow us to recognise the visionary worlds of our “Eastern sages” as having a reality of their own, rather than hiding a refusal to consider them behind explanations drawn from historical studies or sociology. It is not enough, for example, to say that the teachings of Ishraq were developed in the seventeenth century.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00898

Nor does it explain them to say, rather absurdly, that they were “a product of their time,” if by time we mean only the calendar of historical events. So what is being revealed to us in this form of human experience? How is it possible? Perhaps we are trying to rediscover a “lost continent.” Finding it may be as difficult for us as it is for someone studying lived experience to grasp the world that opens through the rhythms of musical space.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00899

It is not only the Bible and the Qur’an that confront us with an undeniable fact: for a great many readers, a text has meanings beyond what its outward words (zahir) appear to say. Much of Persian literature poses the same problem, including mystical epics and lyric poetry. How many Western scholars of the East have been surprised, even scandalised, to discover that so many Iranian readers hear a mystical meaning in the poems of Hafez!
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00900
Yet the fact remains, and no amount of deafness to spiritual meaning can make it go away.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00901

So when I speak of an interpretive perspective, I mean different levels of meaning that correspond to the echoes of the divine Word across different levels of reality. By connecting this with the questions raised by musical perspective, I am not speaking merely in metaphors. I know that the approach I have sketched goes against the prevailing tendencies in theology and the study of Scripture today. More simply, it goes against the world as it appears to what we call historical consciousness.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00902

But further texts will show why we must question the assumptions behind that way of seeing. Otherwise we risk the gravest misunderstandings whenever we try to meet people whose experience of the world still remains open to the perspectives of traditional culture, as is true in parts of Iran even today.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00903

What we call historical development generally moves along a horizontal line. It is guided by a supposed “direction of history,” an idea that has taken hold of so many modern minds almost like a secular religious dogma.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00904

But this way of looking at time goes hand in hand with the loss of another dimension: the dimension of height, the vertical or polar direction. Traditional cultures orient themselves by a “heavenly pole,” a “cosmic north.” The terms mabda' and ma'ad mark two movements along this axis, one descending and the other ascending. Suhrawardi draws attention to this when he says: “You are told: Return!
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00905

“But the very idea of returning means that you were there before. And woe to you if you imagine that the place of your return is Damascus, Baghdad, or any other earthly homeland!” We should therefore ask whether the loss of this vertical dimension is what leaves modern readers facing a false choice whenever they encounter an ancient sacred text: is it myth, or is it history?
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00906

Neither myth nor history. We escape that narrow choice only by accepting that events can be entirely real while taking place in a space other than the physical world, which we usually treat as the only stage on which “historical” events can occur. Our authors developed a remarkably detailed account of the nature of this other space. They called it alam al-mithal, the mundus imaginalis: not an imaginary world, as though it were unreal, but the imaginal world.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00907

I have examined it at greater length elsewhere. Modern readers who pose the choice between myth and history usually assume, without saying so, that what counts as real history must be made up of outward, material facts. They also lump spiritual meaning, symbol, myth, and allegory together without first asking whether they are the same thing. This confusion is everywhere.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00908

What has to happen for a genuine spiritual meaning to be lost and turned into mere allegory? Such a loss is a decline in spiritual forms, closely linked to the disappearance of the vertical, polar dimension we have just described. We need to take our earlier comparison of Christianity and Islam further and ask what conditions each tradition has provided for spiritual interpretation. I noted above that Islam has no institution corresponding to the Christian Church.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00909

We might ask whether the growth of that kind of institution tends to favour literal and historical readings, admitting at most the occasional pious interpretation in which an earlier figure or event stands for a later one, or else a moral allegory. Such readings may be deeply edifying, but they are also harmless to established structures, both in philosophy and in society. In Christianity, the tradition of spiritual interpretation has most often survived and renewed itself among groups outside the official churches. Modern biblical scholarship, however, has frequently dismissed their readings as arbitrary, artificial, or even a violation of the text.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00910

Conditions were different in Islam, as we noted earlier, even though periods of political success could be a trial for Ismaili and Twelver Shiism alike. We would still need to explore why Islamic spiritual thinkers found it possible—or necessary—to resist compromising their personal spiritual demands with collective rules that would turn religion into something governed by society.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00911
Suhrawardi gives this conflict a moving symbolic form in his Tale of the Western Exile (see Book II).
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00912

Another symbol lies in the very word for a person following the spiritual path: the salik, a “pilgrim” travelling through spaces beyond the visible world. It recalls the expression peregrinare pro Christo—to wander or make a pilgrimage for Christ—used in the early Celtic Church.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00913

But every question we have raised here ultimately depends on one greater question: how are the world beyond the senses and the world we can sense related? How can powers beyond matter be present within material forms? And what relationship, if any, exists between spiritual ranks and the hierarchies of earthly society? This is the first and the final question, because it helps explain the different paths taken by the traditional East and by the West.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00914

We find a beautiful account of this relationship between the spiritual and the visible world in the writings of the late Shaykh Sarkar Agha, the leader of the Shaykhi school in Iran. His account fits perfectly with the philosophy of light. When he speaks of souls entering this world, he says we should picture the way a person’s image appears in a mirror.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00915

Or think of sunlight striking a reflecting surface from high above. The burning body of the sun does not literally “come down” to Earth. In the same way, souls—spiritual selves together with their original spiritual bodies—do not physically descend into this world “in person.” The mirror through which a soul appears in earthly life can shatter, but the original image belongs to another world and continues to exist in its own right.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00916

An image’s presence “suspended” in a mirror is nothing like the way blackness, for example, spreads through a black object. The material of the mirror is not the material of the image reflected in it. The mirror shows the image. And by showing it, the mirror reveals that the image is present “elsewhere,” in another dimension. This is pure appearance through light.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00917

Here we find an understanding of being, life, our presence in the world, and its ultimate purpose that differs sharply from what Western readers ordinarily associate with incarnation. This brings us back to an earlier question, and it is a decisive one. What would a world in which the religious doctrine of the Incarnation had never prevailed make of that doctrine’s transformation—or decline—into a secular doctrine of social incarnation, expressed as collective consciousness? Such a doctrine can foster the illusion that merely by leaving behind individual existence we enter something like the divine.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00918

Would the development of the world of Forms follow a parallel path? Shiite inner spirituality has a very different centre of gravity: the ghaybat, the hiddenness of the Hidden Imam. This is an extreme instance of the mystical dimension that surrounds all things and makes them shine with a reality beyond the senses. The fundamental contrast, then, is between historical consciousness and gnostic consciousness: between a way of seeing shaped by outward history and one shaped by inner spiritual knowledge.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
en-book-1-ch-4-s3
3. Historical Consciousness and Gnostic Consciousness
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00919
Historical consciousness is a subject that people today readily accept as important.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00920

But if we want to do justice to gnostic consciousness—a way of knowing through inner spiritual insight—we must move against many of today’s theological currents and break with deeply rooted prejudices. Otherwise we will simply treat it as one more “historical phenomenon,” which would defeat the purpose of our inquiry. Our first warning, whenever the opportunity arises, must be against the common confusion between allegory and spiritual meaning.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00921

The methods Christians used to interpret their sacred writings can teach us much about the beginnings of Qur’anic interpretation. Especially valuable are the different approaches associated with the early schools of Antioch and Alexandria. I cannot review the whole field here; I must refer readers to the major studies of early Christian interpretation and recall the old formula that came to express the famous doctrine of Scripture’s four meanings: littera (sensus historicus) gesta docet; quid credas, allegoria; moralis, quid agas; quid speras, anagogia.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00922

In English: “The letter, or historical meaning, tells you what happened; allegory tells you what to believe; the moral meaning tells you what to do; and the higher, or anagogical, meaning tells you what to hope for.” This formula has a poor reputation today. Even mentioning it can irritate scholars of language and theologians, who see it as a clever but artificial method for twisting texts and forcing them to say what their interpreters already wanted them to say. We have to admit that the method was often abused. It could dissolve a text’s actual content into a universal system of allegorical readings.
